subjects.name: APPLIED CHEMISTRY
course_outcomes: Understand the concepts of fundamental of chemistry and organic chemistry
Will be aware of the basics of reaction mechanism and structure & stability of reacting constituents
Obtain the information regarding the electromotive force and cells
Understand the use of chemistry in our day-to-day life
Identify various electrochemical systems for use in domestic and industrial settings

units.title: Basic Concepts of Chemistry
units.topics: Introduction, Importance of Chemistry, Nature of matter, classification based on physical state, classification based on chemical structure, Physical quantities, atomic mass, molecular mass, molar mass and mole concept, Atomic number, atomic mass, isotope, isobar and isotone. Bohr's atomic model, Quantum numbers, shape of s, p, d and f orbitals, rules of electron arrangement in orbitals.

units.title: General Organic Chemistry
units.topics: Introduction, tetravalency of carbon, hybridization, sp, sp2 and sp3 hybrid orbitals with examples, functional groups, IUPAC nomenclature of organic compounds, inductive effect, main types of organic reactions.

units.title: Electromotive Force
units.topics: Introduction, Types of electrochemical cells and examples, Half- cell, Reversible and irreversible cell, Convention sign, Types of electrodes, cell reactions, Representation of cell, emfof cell, emf series. Thermodynamicderivation of Nernst equation. Standard cells. Half-cells/electrodes, different types ofelectrodes (with examples). Standard electrode potential (IUPAC convention) andprinciples of its determination. Types of cells: electrolytic, galvanic and concentration cells

units.title: Polymers
units.topics: Introduction, classification of polymers, industrial manufacturing, properties and uses of some important polymers: Polythene, Teflon, Polyacrylonitrile, Polyvinyl chloride, Polystyrene Total Hours 28

examTypes.syllabusScope: First 50% syllabus: Basic Concepts of Chemistry; General Organic Chemistry

subjects.name: BHARATIYA KNOWLEDGE SYSTEM
course_outcomes: Describe the structure of Bharatiya Knowledge Systems and recognize key philosophical and literary traditions
Explain ancient Indian developments in mathematics, astronomy, and their relevance to modern science
Identify technological and architectural innovations rooted in ancient Indian practices
Express core Indian philosophies related to the purpose of life, spiritual evolution, and ethical living.

units.title: Introduction to Bharatiya Knowledge Systems (BKS)
units.topics: Definition and classification of BKS, Caturdasa-Vidyasthana, The Vedic Corps & Philosophical Systems (Introduction to the Four Vedas , Vedangas ,Vedic School of Philosophy), Wisdom through the Ages ( Puranas – An Encyclopaedical Work, Itihasa as a Source of Wisdom)

units.title: Science and Mathematics in Ancient Bharat
units.topics: Indian Language Sciences (Components of a Language , Sanskrit and Role of Sanskrit in Natural Language Processing), Number System and Units of Measurement (Number System in India – Historical Evidence , Measurement for Time, Distance and Weight), Mathematics (An overview of the Development of Mathematics in India , Arithmetic, Geometry, Trigonometry and Algebra in Ancient texts), Astronomy ( Vedanga Jyotish , Measuring Time & Calendar)

units.title: Engineering, Technology and Architecture in Ancient Bharat
units.topics: Metallurgy and Textile Technology (Metals and Metalworking Technology ,Iron and Steel Technology ,Textile and Dyeing – Indian Specialities), Irrigation and Water Management (Harappan and Traditional Water Management System of Gujarat , Historical Sites – Sringeverpur, South Indian Water Management System, Rain Water Harvesting System), Sacred Ecology and Environment (Sacred Hills, Mountains and Forest ,Nakshatrara Gyaan and Agriculture,Forest Management and Urban Planning), Transportation ( Modes of Transportations and Reforms, Development of Trading Techniques), Vastu sastra – The Science of Architecture (Town Planning, Civil Architecture ,Temple Architecture)

units.title: Concepts of Life in Ancient Bharat
units.topics: Four Stages of Life , Four Goals of Human Life , Karma & Rebirth, Striving for Moksha Total Hours 28

firstHalfUnits.title: Science and Mathematics in Ancient Bharat

subjects.name: INDIAN CONSTITUTION
course_outcomes: 1. To learn about law enactment and importance of Constitution.
2. To understand the fundamental rights and fundamental duties of the Indian citizen to instill morality, social values, honesty, dignity of life and their social responsibilities.
3. To create awareness of their surroundings, society, social problems and their suitable solutions while keeping rights and duties of the citizen keeping in mind
4. To understand powers and functionalities from union to local self-government.
5. To justify the need for protection of human rights and to know about concept of women empowerment.

units.title: The Constitution – Introduction
units.topics: • Meaning of the constitution law and constitutionalism, • The History of the Making of the Indian Constitution, • Preamble and the Basic Structure, and its Interpretation, • Salient features and characteristics of the Constitution of India, • Fundamental Rights and Duties and their Interpretation, Right to Equality under Article – 14, Right to certain Freedom under Article 19, Scope of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21, Fundamental Duties and its legal status, • State Policy Principles- Its importance and Implementation

units.title: Union Government
units.topics: • Structure of the Indian Union, • President – Role and Power , • Prime Minister and Council of Ministers , • Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha

units.title: State Government
units.topics: • Governor – Role and Power , • Chief Minister and Council of Ministers , • State Secretariat

units.title: Local Administration
units.topics: • District Administration , • Municipal Corporation , • Zila Panchayat

units.title: Election Commission
units.topics: • Role and Functioning , • Chief Election Commissioner , • State Election Commission Total Hours 28

The four Vedas are Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. The Rigveda is known for hymns; the Samaveda is closely associated with chants and melodies; the Yajurveda contains prose formulas and material related to ritual performance; and the Atharvaveda includes hymns and material concerning everyday life and ritual. Questions: [8 marks] Explain Metallurgy and iron/steel technology in historical India. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Traditional textile technology and dyeing. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Water management and rainwater harvesting. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Sacred ecology, forests and agricultural knowledge. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
Answers:
Model answer:
Metallurgy includes obtaining metals from ores and shaping or treating them for use. A historical discussion can cover ore preparation, heating and reduction, forging, joining, heat treatment and the properties sought, while recognizing that techniques varied across periods and regions. Iron and steel production requires evidence about the artifact, process and material; the existence of a notable artifact does not prove that one technique was universal. A well-supported answer connects process to properties such as strength, hardness, corrosion behaviour or workability and identifies the limits of the available evidence.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Textile technology includes fibre preparation, spinning, weaving and finishing. Dyeing adds colour using a dye source and a process suited to the fibre; preparation, temperature, time and mordants can affect shade and colour fastness. Historical Indian textile traditions included sophisticated regional practices, but materials and techniques differed. To analyze a process, identify the fibre, colour source, preparation, application and finishing steps, then explain how these steps influence the result. Avoid treating all traditional dyes or textile methods as chemically or historically identical.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Water management combines collection, storage, distribution, drainage and maintenance. Rainwater harvesting captures runoff from a roof or catchment, conveys it through channels, filters or settles sediment, and stores or recharges it where appropriate. Traditional systems were adapted to local rainfall, terrain, materials and community needs; Gujarat and other regions contain different examples. A useful analysis checks catchment area, water demand, overflow, contamination prevention and maintenance responsibility. Historical systems should be explained in their local setting rather than assumed to work unchanged in every modern site.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Traditional ecological knowledge may connect land, water, forests, seasonal cycles and social or religious practices. A study of Nakshatra-related agricultural knowledge should identify the particular calendar or observational claim and compare it with the local context and available evidence. Forest management and sacred natural sites can also be studied for their cultural meaning and practical conservation effects. Do not assume that every community followed one identical practice or that cultural association alone proves a measurable ecological outcome. Distinguish historical description, current practice and independently tested environmental effects.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

[8 marks] A student must apply traditional textile technology and dyeing in a practical situation such as describing how a natural dye process moves from source material to finished cloth. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply water management and rainwater harvesting in a practical situation such as planning a system for collecting seasonal rainfall in a settlement. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply sacred ecology, forests and agricultural knowledge in a practical situation such as assessing a claim connecting seasonal observations with farm decisions. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.
Answers:
Model answer:
Metallurgy includes obtaining metals from ores and shaping or treating them for use. A historical discussion can cover ore preparation, heating and reduction, forging, joining, heat treatment and the properties sought, while recognizing that techniques varied across periods and regions. Iron and steel production requires evidence about the artifact, process and material; the existence of a notable artifact does not prove that one technique was universal. A well-supported answer connects process to properties such as strength, hardness, corrosion behaviour or workability and identifies the limits of the available evidence.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should connect the concept to the stated example, explain the steps in order and justify the outcome.

Model answer:
Textile technology includes fibre preparation, spinning, weaving and finishing. Dyeing adds colour using a dye source and a process suited to the fibre; preparation, temperature, time and mordants can affect shade and colour fastness. Historical Indian textile traditions included sophisticated regional practices, but materials and techniques differed. To analyze a process, identify the fibre, colour source, preparation, application and finishing steps, then explain how these steps influence the result. Avoid treating all traditional dyes or textile methods as chemically or historically identical.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should connect the concept to the stated example, explain the steps in order and justify the outcome.

Model answer:
Water management combines collection, storage, distribution, drainage and maintenance. Rainwater harvesting captures runoff from a roof or catchment, conveys it through channels, filters or settles sediment, and stores or recharges it where appropriate. Traditional systems were adapted to local rainfall, terrain, materials and community needs; Gujarat and other regions contain different examples. A useful analysis checks catchment area, water demand, overflow, contamination prevention and maintenance responsibility. Historical systems should be explained in their local setting rather than assumed to work unchanged in every modern site.

Questions: [8 marks] Explain Skimming, scanning, intensive and extensive reading. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Reading comprehension and evidence-based answers. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain English tenses and consistency of time. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Parts of speech and their functions. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
Answers:
Model answer:
Skimming is a rapid read to identify the general idea and structure; scanning searches for a specific detail such as a date or name. Intensive reading examines a short passage carefully for meaning, vocabulary and relationships, while extensive reading builds fluency through longer texts for general understanding. Select the technique to match the purpose, preview headings or key words, and return to the passage for evidence before answering. These methods complement rather than replace one another; a reader often skims first, scans for details and then reads a critical section intensively.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Comprehension requires identifying the central idea, supporting details, sequence, purpose, tone and implied meaning. Direct questions can often be answered from an explicit sentence; inference questions require connecting evidence and background understanding without inventing facts. Read the question carefully, locate relevant lines, distinguish fact from opinion and summarize in one's own words when appropriate. A correct answer should be supported by the passage, not merely by personal belief. For unfamiliar vocabulary, use surrounding sentences and word structure as clues, then verify the interpretation in context.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Tense and aspect locate an action in time and describe whether it is ongoing, completed or connected to another time. Simple forms express facts or events; continuous forms emphasize duration; perfect forms connect an earlier action with a reference time. Maintain consistent time references unless the meaning requires a shift. For example, a report of a completed visit generally uses past forms for events, while a general conclusion may use present tense. Check time expressions and the intended chronology when choosing a verb form.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Nouns name people, places, things or ideas; pronouns replace noun phrases; verbs express actions or states; adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs. [8 marks] Explain Planning and writing a clear formal email. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Structure and tone of a formal application. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Writing an event or industrial-visit report. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Planning and organizing an assignment. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
Answers:
Model answer:
A formal email needs a specific subject line, an appropriate greeting, a concise opening that states the purpose, organized details, a clear request or next step, a courteous closing and the sender's name. Use a professional tone, correct grammar and paragraphs that each serve one purpose. Check the recipient address and any attachment before sending. Add CC only for people who need visibility and BCC when recipients should not see one another's addresses. Do not place confidential information in unnecessary recipients or subject lines.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
A formal application identifies the recipient, date, subject and applicant, then states the request clearly and gives only relevant reasons or supporting details. It uses a respectful salutation, concise body paragraphs, a clear closing and the required signature or identification. The writer should maintain a formal tone, avoid slang and emotional exaggeration, and ensure the requested action is explicit. Proofread names, dates and attachments. A good application lets the recipient understand what is being requested, why it is justified and what response or approval is needed.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
A report records an event objectively and in a structured order. Include a meaningful title, date and place, purpose, participants, major activities, observations, outcomes and a conclusion or recommendations where appropriate. Arrange events chronologically or under clear headings and use past tense for completed activities. Separate observed facts from personal opinion and support claims with reliable details. Proofread names and dates, keep the language concise, and make the report useful to a reader who did not attend the event.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Begin by interpreting the task and identifying the expected scope. Gather relevant sources, make an outline, and organize the introduction, main discussion and conclusion in a logical sequence. Each paragraph should develop one idea and connect it to the overall argument. Use accurate examples and acknowledge sources in the required format; do not copy text without attribution. Revise for completeness, flow, factual accuracy and grammar, then check formatting and submission requirements. A strong assignment answers the exact question rather than merely collecting loosely related information.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Questions: [8 marks] A student must apply planning and writing a clear formal email in a practical situation such as requesting a meeting with a faculty member about a lab submission. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply structure and tone of a formal application in a practical situation such as applying for permission to attend an academic event. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply writing an event or industrial-visit report in a practical situation such as reporting a college visit with observations and outcomes. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply planning and organizing an assignment in a practical situation such as turning a broad topic into a well-structured short assignment. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.
Answers:
Model answer:
A formal email needs a specific subject line, an appropriate greeting, a concise opening that states the purpose, organized details, a clear request or next step, a courteous closing and the sender's name. Use a professional tone, correct grammar and paragraphs that each serve one purpose. Check the recipient address and any attachment before sending. Add CC only for people who need visibility and BCC when recipients should not see one another's addresses. Do not place confidential information in unnecessary recipients or subject lines.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should connect the concept to the stated example, explain the steps in order and justify the outcome.

Model answer:
A formal application identifies the recipient, date, subject and applicant, then states the request clearly and gives only relevant reasons or supporting details. It uses a respectful salutation, concise body paragraphs, a clear closing and the required signature or identification. The writer should maintain a formal tone, avoid slang and emotional exaggeration, and ensure the requested action is explicit. Proofread names, dates and attachments. A good application lets the recipient understand what is being requested, why it is justified and what response or approval is needed.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should connect the concept to the stated example, explain the steps in order and justify the outcome.

Model answer:
A report records an event objectively and in a structured order. Include a meaningful title, date and place, purpose, participants, major activities, observations, outcomes and a conclusion or recommendations where appropriate. Arrange events chronologically or under clear headings and use past tense for completed activities. Separate observed facts from personal opinion and support claims with reliable details. Proofread names and dates, keep the language concise, and make the report useful to a reader who did not attend the event.

Questions: [8 marks] Explain Number sets and laws of indices. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain HCF and LCM of integers. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain HCF and LCM of fractions and decimals. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Polynomial definitions and arithmetic operations. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
Answers:
Model answer:
Number sets include natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers and real numbers, with each set having specific membership rules. For a non-zero base a, powers follow laws such as a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), and a^0 = 1. These laws require attention to conditions such as non-zero denominators and the base not being zero for a^0. For example, 2^3 × 2^4 ÷ 2^5 = 2^(3+4−5) = 2^2 = 4.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
The HCF is the greatest positive integer that divides every given integer; the LCM is the smallest positive common multiple. Prime factorization is a reliable method: 12 = 2^2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3^2. For HCF, take common prime factors with the smallest exponents, giving 2 × 3 = 6. For LCM, take each prime factor with the greatest exponent, giving 2^2 × 3^2 = 36. For positive integers, HCF × LCM equals the product of the two integers.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
First express fractions in their lowest terms. For positive fractions, the usual course rules are HCF = HCF of numerators divided by LCM of denominators, and LCM = LCM of numerators divided by HCF of denominators. Thus for 2/3 and 4/5, HCF = 2/15 and LCM = 4. For decimals, convert values to integers by multiplying by an appropriate power of ten, find the HCF/LCM, then rescale the result. Keep the decimal-place adjustment consistent and verify the resulting multiples or divisors.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
A polynomial is an expression formed from constants and variables with non-negative integer exponents and coefficients. Like terms have the same variable part and exponents, so only their coefficients are combined. For example, (2x + 3) + (x − 5) = 3x − 2. The degree of a non-zero polynomial in one variable is the highest exponent with a non-zero coefficient; the degree of 3x^4 − 2x^2 + 7 is four. Keep signs and exponents unchanged while grouping terms, and simplify before identifying the degree.

Questions: [8 marks] A student must apply number sets and laws of indices in a practical situation such as simplifying a product and quotient of powers with the same non-zero base. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply hcf and lcm of integers in a practical situation such as finding the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply hcf and lcm of fractions and decimals in a practical situation such as finding HCF and LCM for 2/3 and 4/5 after simplifying the fractions. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.

[8 marks] A student must apply polynomial definitions and arithmetic operations in a practical situation such as simplifying (2x + 3) + (x − 5) and identifying degree. Explain the method or reasoning, set out the main steps, and justify the result.
Answers:
Model answer:
Number sets include natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers and real numbers, with each set having specific membership rules. For a non-zero base a, powers follow laws such as a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), and a^0 = 1. These laws require attention to conditions such as non-zero denominators and the base not being zero for a^0. For example, 2^3 × 2^4 ÷ 2^5 = 2^(3+4−5) = 2^2 = 4.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should connect the concept to the stated example, explain the steps in order and justify the outcome.

Model answer:
The HCF is the greatest positive integer that divides every given integer; the LCM is the smallest positive common multiple. Prime factorization is a reliable method: 12 = 2^2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3^2. For HCF, take common prime factors with the smallest exponents, giving 2 × 3 = 6. For LCM, take each prime factor with the greatest exponent, giving 2^2 × 3^2 = 36. For positive integers, HCF × LCM equals the product of the two integers.

Questions: [8 marks] Explain Number sets and laws of indices. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain HCF and LCM of integers, fractions and decimals. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Polynomial arithmetic and algebraic identities. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
[8 marks] Explain Area and perimeter of 2D shapes. Describe its meaning or purpose, principal features or steps, and one relevant example.
Answers:
Model answer:
Classify numbers carefully: integers include negative whole-number values, rational numbers can be expressed as a ratio of integers with non-zero denominator, irrational values cannot be so expressed, and real numbers include rational and irrational values. For a non-zero base a, use a^m a^n = a^(m+n), a^m/a^n = a^(m−n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), and a^0 = 1. State domain restrictions and simplify stepwise; exponents add when multiplying like bases and subtract when dividing them.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
For integers, prime-factorize and use minimum exponents for HCF and maximum exponents for LCM. For positive fractions in lowest terms, use HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators) for HCF, and LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators) for LCM. For decimals, scale all values by the same power of ten to make integers, calculate HCF or LCM, then reverse the scale. Example: HCF(12,18)=6 and LCM(12,18)=36. Check that the HCF divides the original integers and the LCM is a common multiple.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Combine only like terms, preserve signs, and use the highest non-zero exponent to determine degree. Common identities include (a+b)^2=a²+2ab+b², (a−b)^2=a²−2ab+b² and (a+b)(a−b)=a²−b². For example, (x+3)^2=x²+6x+9; the 6x middle term comes from both cross-products. Use identities to expand or factor efficiently, and verify by substitution of a convenient value when checking a potentially incorrect expression.

8-mark marking guide: 2 marks for the core concept; 3 marks for accurate principles, steps or formulas; 2 marks for an example/application; 1 mark for a justified conclusion or check. A strong answer should define the concept and organize the main points clearly.

Model answer:
Use a formula matched to the geometry and label the dimensions. Perimeter uses linear units and area uses square units. Use perpendicular height where required and do not substitute a sloping side for height.
